Secrets API: encrypted, versioned storage for credentials
_description:
The [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/08/25/proposal-a-secrets-api-for-wordpress-7-2/ Secrets API proposal] is for a core API that stores credentials such as API keys and tokens encrypted at rest, keeps a previous version for rotation, and lets hosts replace the storage through a `secrets.php` drop-in. This ticket covers the 7.2 part: the API itself. The admin screen is deferred to 7.3, as the proposal says. The WP-CLI commands stay in the feature plugin for now, since WP-CLI commands ship as WP-CLI packages rather than in core.

The patch is the `src/` directory of the [https://github.com/ericmann/secrets-api feature plugin], copied without changes, plus the wiring the plugin's bootstrap does today. The plugin has been public since 4 September and is at v0.2.0. The documentation, including every place the code departs from the proposal and why, is at [https://secretsapi.dev/ secretsapi.dev].

This is also the storage #64789 asks for. The Connectors screen from #64730 keeps AI provider API keys as plaintext options, which are visible on `options.php`. Stored through this API, they are encrypted under a key that is not in the database, so a database dump or backup no longer exposes them. Moving Connectors onto `wp_set_secret()` and `wp_get_secret()` can follow once this lands.

=== The patch ===

 * **The API:** 14 new files in `src/wp-includes/`.
   * the public functions
   * `WP_Secret` and `WP_Secret_Version`
   * the provider, store and keyring interfaces, with their default and fail-closed implementations
   * the cipher and the key manager

   `src/wp-admin/includes/secrets-site-health.php` adds three Site Health tests and a debug-information section.
 * **Loading:** `wp-settings.php` loads the API, then loads `wp-content/secrets.php` through a new `wp_load_secrets_dropin()` in `load.php`, just before must-use plugins.
 * **Failing closed:** if the drop-in throws, or sets a provider, store or keyring that does not implement its interface, every Secrets API call returns `WP_Error` for the rest of the request. Nothing falls back to the default provider: a broken drop-in has to read as unreachable, never as "this secret does not exist". See [https://secretsapi.dev/decisions/0007-fail-closed-on-a-broken-drop-in/ ADR 0007].
 * **Capabilities:** `populate_roles_720()` grants `manage_secrets` to administrators on install, and `upgrade_720()` grants it on upgrade. `manage_network_secrets` joins the other network capabilities in `map_meta_cap()`, so only super admins hold it.
 * **Tests:** the plugin's tests for everything in `src/`, 371 of them, in `tests/phpunit/tests/secrets/`. They come with provider and keyring conformance suites for hosts that write drop-ins.

=== Changes and additions beyond the proposal ===

The proposal names `wp_set_secret()`, `wp_get_secret()`, `wp_delete_secret()`, `wp_import_option_as_secret()`, `WP_Secret`, and `WP_Secret_Version`. Everything below differs from or goes beyond that, and is listed so each item can be reviewed, and rejected, on its own. The reasoning for each is on the linked page.

 * `WP_Secret::reveal()` returns `string|WP_Error`, not `string`: [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/retrieval/ retrieval]
 * `wp_retire_secret_version()` and `wp_list_secrets()`: [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/rotation/ rotation], [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/retrieval/ retrieval]
 * Network scope, which the proposal describes without naming functions: `wp_set_network_secret()`, `wp_get_network_secret()`, `wp_delete_network_secret()`, `wp_retire_network_secret_version()`, `wp_list_network_secrets()`. See [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/network/ network].
 * `wp_secrets_validate_name()`, `wp_secrets_memzero()`, `wp_using_secrets_dropin()`, `wp_secrets_provider_is_writable()`, `wp_secrets_provider_label()`
 * The `wp_secret_changed` action, for auditing, plus `WP_Secret::get_name()` and `WP_Secret::withheld()`
 * The `WP_Secrets_Provider`, `WP_Secrets_Store`, and `WP_Secrets_Keyring` interfaces, and their default and fail-closed implementations. The provider replaced the proposal's two-part drop-in contract after hosts on the proposal thread showed it could not describe how they already deploy. See [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/providers-and-keyrings/ providers and keyrings] and [https://secretsapi.dev/decisions/0001-provider-as-outermost-extension-point/ ADR 0001].
 * Constants: ten `WP_SECRETS_ERROR_*` codes, `WP_SECRETS_RECORD_VERSION`, `WP_SECRETS_MAX_NAME_LENGTH`, `WP_SECRETS_CAP_MANAGE`, and `WP_SECRETS_CAP_MANAGE_NETWORK`

The [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/scope/ scope page] has the complete list.

=== Testing ===

 * **In this branch:**
   * `npm run test:php -- --group secrets` passes on single site and multisite (371 tests each).
   * `tests/phpunit/tests/user/capabilities.php` passes with both capabilities added to its inventory.
   * The full single-site suite shows no new failures.
 * **The plugin's CI:** PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.3, each against WordPress latest and trunk, plus a multisite job and a WP-CLI smoke test on PHP 7.4 and 8.3.

summary: After uploading a plugin zip, link to the Plugin settings instead of the "Plugin Installer"
_description:
After a plugin is installed by uploading a zip (Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin), the result screen shows "Activate Plugin", and once that's done a "Go to Plugin Installer" link pointing to `plugin-install.php`.

Nobody who just uploaded a plugin needs the Plugin Installer next :)

They uploaded a zip, so they weren't browsing the directory. The useful place to go is the Plugin's settings page (?). 

"Go to Plugin Installer" is the only way off the screen, and it goes to the wrong place.

=== History

Before [37221] (#35429, 4.6), uploads fell through to the default "Return to Plugins page" link. That changeset moved the upload form from its own page onto the Add Plugins screen and added a dedicated `'upload' === $this->type && 'plugins' === $from` branch pointing back to the installer. That branch seems to exist only to send users back to where the form now lives. Now that the upload form is a toggle on the installer screen, going back there has no purpose.

=== Proposed fix

Remove that branch from `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()` so uploads use the existing `else` branch, "Go to Plugins page" (`plugins.php`).

Installs from the directory (`'web'`) keep "Go to Plugin Installer", since people often install several plugins in a row there. The importer flow is unchanged. There are no new strings, and sites can still change the link through the `install_plugin_complete_actions` filter.

Patch attached.

=== Testing instructions

 1. Go to Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin and upload any valid plugin zip.
 2. On the result screen, confirm the secondary link reads "Go to Plugins page" and opens `plugins.php`.
 3. Install a plugin from the directory with JS disabled (`update.php?action=install-plugin`) and confirm it still shows "Go to Plugin Installer".

=== Related

 - #35429: moved the upload form onto the Add Plugins screen and introduced the installer link for uploads.
 - #60578: added the installer link to the upload error screen, a different case where the link makes sense.
 - #66184: same result screen, Activate button with unmet plugin dependencies.
 - #40651: finding plugin settings after activation, which would be the natural next step beyond this fix.

summary: Add NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES to wpdb::$incompatible_modes
_description:
When the MySQL/MariaDB `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` SQL mode is enabled, the backslash (`\`) is treated as an ordinary character inside string literals instead of as an escape character.

WordPress assumes backslash escaping in many places, both in core and in the plugin/theme ecosystem. With this mode active, a literal such as `'It\'s'` is no longer read as `It's`. The quote ends the string early, and the query either fails with a syntax error or stores or matches the wrong value.

This is a long-known incompatibility that has come up several times over the years: #2820, #3286, #57149.

`wpdb::set_sql_mode()` already strips SQL modes that WordPress is known not to support, through `wpdb::$incompatible_modes`:

{{{#!php
protected $incompatible_modes = array(
	'NO_ZERO_DATE',
	'ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY',
	'STRICT_TRANS_TABLES',
	'STRICT_ALL_TABLES',
	'TRADITIONAL',
	'ANSI',
);
}}}

`NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` is not on that list. If the server or a hosting environment sets it globally, WordPress keeps it for the session, and queries fail.

To fix this, we should add `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` to `wpdb::$incompatible_modes`, so WordPress removes it from the session SQL mode like the other modes it doesn't support. Sites that really need the mode can still re-enable it with the existing `incompatible_sql_modes` filter.

summary: After uploading a plugin that "requires" other plugins, the "Activate Plugin" button leads to a wp_die() WSOD
_description:
When a plugin is installed by uploading a zip, the result screen always shows an "Activate Plugin" button, even when the plugin's `Requires Plugins` header lists plugins that are not installed or not active. Clicking it takes the user to a bare `wp_die()` white screen with no admin menu and no way forward other than the browser's back button or the "Manage plugins" link.

[[Image()]]

The Plugins list table and the AJAX install flow already block activation in this case (the AJAX flow since #61294). The installer screen should behave the same way.

== Steps to reproduce

1. Create a plugin with this header and zip it:

{{{
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Dep Test Plugin
 * Requires Plugins: classic-editor
 */
}}}

2. Make sure the required plugin (Classic Editor in this example) is not installed on the site
3. Go to Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin and install the zip.
4. On the result screen, click "Activate Plugin".

**Actual result:** a `wp_die()` white screen reading "Error: Dep Test Plugin requires 1 plugin to be installed and activated: Classic Editor. Manage plugins."

**Expected result:** the result screen does not offer "Activate Plugin" (or "Network Activate" on multisite) and tells the user which plugins are missing, inside the normal admin screen.

== Cause

Uploads and non-JS installs run through `update.php?action=upload-plugin` and `update.php?action=install-plugin`, which render `Plugin_Installer_Skin`. `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()` builds the activate links based only on the install result, the `activate_plugin` capability and whether the plugin is already active. It never checks the plugin's requirements, and `update.php` never initializes `WP_Plugin_Dependencies`.

The link goes to `plugins.php?action=activate`, where `activate_plugin()` calls `validate_plugin_requirements()`, gets a `plugin_missing_dependencies` error, and `plugins.php` passes it to `wp_die()`.

== Proposed fix

In `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()`, when the install succeeded and the user can activate the plugin, call `validate_plugin_requirements()`, the same check `activate_plugin()` runs. If it returns a `WP_Error`, remove the activate and network activate links and show the error message as an admin notice.

`validate_plugin_requirements()` already calls `WP_Plugin_Dependencies::initialize()`, and `Plugin_Upgrader::install()` has already cleared the plugins cache, so the newly installed plugin's header is read correctly. Reusing this function also means the installer screen never offers a link that `activate_plugin()` would reject, including the WordPress and PHP version checks and the `validate_plugin_requirements` filter.

Patch attached.

== Testing instructions

1. Apply the patch.
2. Repeat the steps to reproduce above.
3. Confirm the result screen shows an error notice naming the missing plugin and no "Activate Plugin" button.
4. Upload a plugin without a `Requires Plugins` header and confirm "Activate Plugin" still appears.
5. Optional: repeat on multisite from Network Admin and confirm "Network Activate" is hidden only in the unmet-dependency case.

== Related

* #61294: the same bug in the AJAX install flow, fixed in 6.5.4 by adding a missed `initialize()` call.
* #64493: improving plugin dependency messages (7.2).
* #22316: the original Plugin Dependencies feature, shipped in 6.5.

summary: Add grunt ticket:<n> to read a Trac ticket, and restore grunt patch:<n>, by fetching through the Playwright browser core already ships
_description:
core.trac.wordpress.org now answers every non-browser request with a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge (`Checking your browser...`, HTTP 403). That includes the plain HTML, `?format=rss`, `?format=csv`, the attachment listing, and raw attachments. Two consequences for contributors and committers:

 1. `grunt patch:<ticket>` fails for every ticket. Reproduced today against #66079: {{{Running "patch:66079" (patch) task >> getPatchFromTicket fail >> status: 403}}}. This is tracked upstream as [https://github.com/WordPress/grunt-patch-wordpress/issues/210 grunt-patch-wordpress#210] (August 2026), with no fix.
 2. There is no way to read a ticket from the command line at all. Anyone scripting a triage or commit workflow, including AI-assisted ones, has to paste ticket text by hand.

The durable fix is a structured read API, proposed in [https://meta.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/8202 meta:#8202]. That ticket is currently unowned (owner removed June 2026) and the discussion there favours either Systems restoring access for identified clients or a Trac-native MCP plugin. Neither is on a timeline.

== Proposal ==

core already ships a real browser: `@playwright/test` 1.61.1 is a devDependency, and the end-to-end and performance workflows install Chromium with `npm exec --no -- playwright install chromium`. The challenge is designed to let browsers through, so a headless Chromium page passes it in a few seconds and can then read the rendered ticket, the attachment list, and raw attachments.

Two tasks, both implemented in the `grunt-patch-wordpress` package that core already depends on, then picked up here with a dependency bump:

 * `grunt ticket:<n>` (new): prints the ticket summary, properties, description, attachments with raw URLs, linked pull requests, and the full change history. `--json` for structured output.
 * `grunt patch:<n>` (existing): swap the two `request()` calls in `getPatchFromTicket()` and `getPatch()` for fetches made through the same Playwright page, so the attachment listing and download work again. Also make the failure message say "Trac returned a bot-protection challenge" instead of "Nothing to patch", as issue 210 asks.

Prerequisite for both: `npx playwright install chromium` once, the same step the e2e suite needs. If no browser is installed the task should say exactly that and exit, not fall through to the old usage help.

A working proof of concept for the read half is at [https://github.com/whyisjake/trac-ticket whyisjake/trac-ticket]. It reads core and meta tickets, keeps the challenge cookie across runs, and takes about 6 seconds per ticket.

== Caveats worth deciding up front ==

 * This routes tooling through a protection Systems put in place. It is the project's own tool on the project's own Trac, using the exact path the challenge is meant to allow, but Systems should be looped in so they are not surprised by headless-browser traffic from committers. An allowlisted client would make all of this unnecessary.
 * It is a stopgap. When meta:#8202 or an equivalent API lands, both tasks should switch to it and drop the browser dependency.
 * Downloading Chromium is roughly 95 MB. That is already true for contributors running e2e tests; it becomes true for anyone who wants `grunt patch` back.

== Related ==

 * [https://github.com/WordPress/grunt-patch-wordpress/issues/210 grunt-patch-wordpress#210] – grunt patch fails for every ticket
 * [https://github.com/WordPress/grunt-patch-wordpress/issues/83 grunt-patch-wordpress#83] – list PRs along with patches (the new task covers this)
 * meta:#8202 – structured JSON API for Trac

AI assistance: Yes. Tool(s): Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1). Used for: confirming the 403 behaviour and the grunt patch failure, locating the upstream issue and meta ticket, building the proof-of-concept script, and drafting this ticket.

Toolbar: free horizontal space on the right side
_description:
This ticket proposes to make the account menu item narrower, so the right side of the Toolbar has more space. The panel underneath stays the same.

=== Current behavior ===

The account item on the right side of the Toolbar is the widest text element in the bar. It shows a full sentence with the display name, plus the avatar.

The right side is also where plugins and hosts add their own items (notifications, site status, account links). As more items land there, the space gets tight. Long display names and long translations make it tighter.

On small screens Core already reduces this item to the avatar only. So the bar works well with a narrower account item.

=== Proposal ===

Show only the display name and the avatar in the bar. The ful l sentence moves inside the panel, next to the avatar, the username and the profile links.

[[Image(toolbar-proposed-crop.png)]]

=== Why ===

 * More space on the right side. The account item gets around 50px narrower in English and more in many languages. That space goes to the items that need it.
 * Clearer control. I believe the name and the avatar are enough to read as "your account". It is the same pattern used by most products.
 * Better fit for long names and long translations. Less truncation and wrapping in the bar.
 * Consistent with small screens, where Core already narrows this item.

=== Accessibility ===

 * The accessible name of the account control becomes the display name. Shorter and clearer for screen reader users.
 * Keyboard and focus behavior does not change. Same menu, same items.
 * The full sentence is still available to everyone who opens the panel.
 * RTL: no change, the text mirrors as today.

=== Backward compatibility ===

 * Existing strings and translations stay in place.
 * Node IDs and the menu structure stay the same. Plugins that add items to the account panel keep working.
 * Sites that customize the account item text with the `gettext` filter keep working.

=== Related ===

 * #48894 improvements to the account panel.
 * #61615 crowding on the right side of the Toolbar.

summary: Default Navigation fallback menu title is ambiguous and produces a redundant accessible name
_description:
== Description

On a fresh WordPress site using a block theme, when there is no existing Navigation Menu or suitable Classic Menu, {{{WP_Navigation_Fallback::create_default_fallback()}}} creates a published {{{wp_navigation}}} post titled “Navigation”:

{{{#!php
'post_title' => _x( 'Navigation', 'Title of a Navigation menu' ),
'post_name'  => 'navigation',
}}}

Source: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/class-wp-navigation-fallback.php#L270-L284 class-wp-navigation-fallback.php]

This causes two related problems:

1. In the Site Editor, “Navigation” is both the name of the Navigation screen and the title of the default menu. The generic menu title does not distinguish the menu from the screen or describe the menu's purpose.
2. The Navigation post title is also used as the frontend navigation landmark's accessible name when the block has no explicit {{{ariaLabel}}}. {{{WP_Navigation_Block_Renderer::get_navigation_name()}}} returns the post title, which is then output as the {{{aria-label}}} on the {{{<nav>}}} element.

Relevant code:

* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/blocks/navigation.php#L583-L605 get_navigation_name()]
* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/blocks/navigation.php#L907-L919 aria-label output]

The resulting markup includes:

{{{
<nav class="wp-block-navigation …" aria-label="Navigation">
}}}

Because the {{{<nav>}}} element already exposes the navigation landmark role, assistive technology may announce this as “Navigation, navigation.” The label is redundant rather than meaningfully distinguishing this landmark from other navigation landmarks.

== Steps to reproduce

1. Start with a fresh WordPress installation using a block theme, with no existing {{{wp_navigation}}} posts or Classic Menus.
2. Open the Site Editor and access the Navigation screen, causing the default fallback Navigation Menu to be created.
3. Observe that the menu is titled “Navigation,” the same name used for the screen.
4. View the site frontend and inspect the Navigation block's {{{<nav>}}} element.
5. Observe {{{aria-label="Navigation"}}}.

== Expected result

The generated menu should have a meaningful administrative title that distinguishes it from the Navigation screen, and the frontend navigation landmark should have a meaningful, non-redundant accessible name.

One possible approach would be to name the administrative object “Primary", which would use “Primary” as the accessible label. 

== Actual result

The generated menu is titled “Navigation,” which is ambiguous in the editor and becomes a redundant accessible name on the frontend.

== Related issues

* #47123 established that navigation landmark labels should not include the word “Navigation,” because screen readers already announce the landmark role.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/59706 Gutenberg #59706] tracks the broader need for meaningful and unique Navigation Menu names and notes that automatically generated names are currently inadequate.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/52488 Gutenberg #52488] tracks broader improvements to Navigation fallback behavior.

summary: Protect wp-content/upgrade-temp-backup (and wp-content/upgrade) from being served over HTTP
_description:
I reported this to the WordPress security team as HackerOne #3993590. John closed it as N/A — not a vulnerability — and said I was welcome to open it here, with the caveat that even a bug report might not really apply, and that a Site Health check could help. So this is a hardening request. Rollback stays.

== What happens ==

Since 6.3, every plugin/theme update moves the previous copy into `wp-content/upgrade-temp-backup/{plugins,themes}/<slug>/` (`WP_Upgrader::move_to_temp_backup_dir()`, `@since 6.3.0`). Unpack staging lives in `wp-content/upgrade/`. Both directories sit in the docroot. `mkdir()` does not drop an `index.php` stub or an `.htaccess`. Core already writes `index.php` (`// Silence is golden.`) into `wp-content/`, `wp-content/plugins/`, `wp-content/themes/`, and `wp-content/uploads/`.

Site Health only checks that the temp-backup directory is writable (`update_temp_backup_writable`). It does not check whether leftovers are web-reachable.

Related: #51857, [55720] (path moved from `upgrade/temp-backup/` to `upgrade-temp-backup/`). See also #64510 (open) — leftovers not deleted when the filesystem is used without `WP_Filesystem` credentials. That ticket is about cleanup. This one is about the copy being HTTP-reachable while it exists.

== What I measured ==

* Healthy update, not a crash: Query Monitor 3.20.2 → 4.0.7. The complete previous version (165 files) was HTTP-reachable for about 2.5 seconds, then deleted on shutdown. The weekly cleanup cron cannot cover this window — it exists on every update.
* Leftovers when cleanup does not run: a failed Forminator auto-update left the previous version (1.35.0) answering HTTP 200 for nine days (`forminator.php` + `readme.txt`). WP-Cron was not firing on that site. `readme.txt` discloses the exact vintage.
* Direct PHP execution: on an nginx + php-fpm origin, a planted `.php` under that path returned 200 and ran. Plugin bootstraps that guard on `ABSPATH` no-op on a direct hit; self-contained handlers (file managers, sanitizers, uploaders) do run. Path-keyed WAF rules aimed at `/wp-content/plugins/<slug>/` miss this URL.

I am not claiming a CVE. Execution is conditional. Version/source disclosure of the previous copy is the thing that always happens while the copy exists.

== What I'd like core to consider ==

Cheapest first:

1. Drop the same `index.php` stub core already uses, when these directories are created. Stops listing. Does not stop a direct file request.
2. Drop an `.htaccess` deny (`Require all denied` / `RedirectMatch 404`) next to it, for Apache and LiteSpeed. nginx still needs a vhost rule.
3. A Site Health check for leftover copies in `upgrade-temp-backup/` — the idea John floated.

I already deny both paths at nginx on my own sites (`location ^~`). Default installs get nothing.

Happy to write a patch for (1) and (3) if this is wanted.

summary: Connectors API: a documented connector type for AI services the AI Client does not drive
_description:
`WP_Connector_Registry::register()` documents one value for `type`, `ai_provider`, which is special-cased: the key is handed to the PHP AI Client and validated on save, and reset when validation fails (https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13031 describes the re-validation). A non-generative AI service, one that returns probabilities and confidence rather than text, cannot pass that validation, so registering it as `ai_provider` would clear a working key.

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/64791 established that plugin-defined types are intended (its use cases include "add a non-AI connector"), and that works: registering under a type of one's own renders the card in its own group on Settings › Connectors, the key is stored and masked by core, and it resolves with the usual env/constant/option precedence. Two gaps remain:

 1. The `register()` docblock still reads as if `ai_provider` were the vocabulary: `@type string $type Required. The connector type, e.g. 'ai_provider'.` Nothing states that other values are supported or how the Connectors screen treats them.

 2. An AI service outside the AI Client is neither `ai_provider` nor a plain non-AI service, and there is no name for it. Each such plugin invents a type, and the screen groups by type, so two judgement-model connectors from two authors would land under two headings. A documented core value (`ai_service`, or whatever name fits) would let them group together, and would give the AI plugin something to recognise when it decides whether AI credentials exist.

Ask: document that plugin-defined types are supported, and add or name one for AI services the AI Client does not drive.

Working example: https://github.com/juanlentino/jev-connector, registered as `ai_decision`, verified on 7.1. Companion request on the PHP AI Client side, for a capability that would let such models be first-class there: https://github.com/WordPress/php-ai-client/issues/296.

summary: Regression in WP 7.1.1: WooCommerce product archives do not render ul.products container
_description:
== Summary ==
After updating WordPress from 7.1 to 7.1.1, WooCommerce product category archives stop rendering the standard <ul class="products"> container. Pagination counts remain correct (e.g. "Showing 1-8 of 25 results"), but no product grid is output in the HTML. Confirmed on desktop and mobile.

== Environment ==
- WordPress: 7.1.1 (broken) vs 7.1 (working)
- WooCommerce: 11.1.1
- PHP: 8.4.24
- MySQL: MariaDB 10.11.18
- Theme: Fashion (Divi child theme, Destaca Imagen)
- Host: IONOS managed WordPress

== Steps to reproduce ==
1. Set up a WooCommerce store on WP 7.1.1 with any theme that renders product archives via WooCommerce's default loop.
2. Navigate to any product category archive (e.g. /categoria-producto/example/).
3. Inspect the DOM with DevTools.
4. Search for "ul.products" in the Elements panel.

== Expected ==
The archive renders a <ul class="products"> containing <li class="product"> entries, one per product in the current pagination page.

== Actual ==
No <ul class="products"> element exists in the DOM. DevTools search returns 0 results. The page renders header, breadcrumbs, page title, and footer, but the product grid container is completely absent.

== Additional evidence ==
A staging site restored from a backup taken on WP 7.1 (with the same WooCommerce, same theme, same plugins, same database) shows the product grid working correctly. The only difference between the two environments is the WordPress core version (7.1 vs 7.1.1).

- Live (WP 7.1.1): grid broken.
- Staging (WP 7.1): grid works.

== Impact ==
This is affecting a live e-commerce store. It appears to be a widespread regression affecting any WooCommerce store updated to WP 7.1.1, regardless of theme or plugin combination. Several users have reported similar issues in the WordPress.org support forums.

== Request ==
Please prioritise a patch for WP 7.1.2. The regression likely lies in how the core handles archive WP_Query objects or in the rendering pipeline introduced/changed in 7.1.1.

Happy to provide access to a staging environment with both versions for debugging purposes.

summary: Empty custom date/time fields are saved instead of remaining null in WordPress 7.1.1
_description:

Go to Settings → General.
Locate the Date Format or Time Format setting.
Select the Custom option.
Leave the custom date/time input field completely blank.
Click Save Changes.
Check the saved setting value.
Actual result

The settings are saved even though the custom date/time field is empty.

An empty custom value is stored instead of leaving the setting as null.

Expected result

If the custom date/time field is empty, WordPress should not save an empty custom value.

The corresponding setting should remain null until a valid custom date/time format is provided.

Regression

This behavior was resolved in WordPress 7.1, but appears to have regressed in WordPress 7.1.1.

Environment

Tested on: [Browser]
PHP: [PHP version]

summary: wp-exclude-emoji is ignored when the excluded element is the node being parsed
_description:
#52219 made `wp-emoji.js` skip elements with the `wp-exclude-emoji` class ([55186]) through a `doNotParse()` callback added to `twemoji.js`. That callback is only consulted in `grabAllTextNodes()`, for the child elements of the node passed to `parse()`. The node passed to `parse()` itself is never checked.

The `MutationObserver` in `wp-emoji.js` passes exactly such a node: for an added text node it moves up to the parent and calls `parse( node )` on it. So an excluded element is parsed, and its emoji replaced, whenever it becomes that node:

* the excluded element itself is inserted after the page has loaded, or
* its own text is replaced, for example with `textContent`.

To reproduce, load a front-end page where the emoji fallback script is active (on current releases #66104 makes that every browser; otherwise one where a support test fails, such as Chromium on Windows for `flag`) and run in the console:

{{{
const span = document.createElement( 'span' );
span.className = 'wp-exclude-emoji';
span.textContent = '\uD83C\uDDF0\uD83C\uDDF7'; // Flag: South Korea
document.body.appendChild( span );
}}}

After the observer runs, the span contains an `img.emoji` whose `alt` is the original South Korea flag and whose `src` is `https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f1f0-1f1f7.svg`.

What I measured on a local page in Chromium on Windows with Core's `wp-emoji.js`, `twemoji.js` and `emoji-loader.js` (with the #66104 patch, so only `flag` failed), counting `img.emoji` after 1.5 seconds:

||= Case =||= Images =||
|| `span.wp-exclude-emoji` in the initial HTML || 0 ||
|| the same span appended after load || 1 ||
|| the initial span's `textContent` replaced || 1 ||
|| `div > p > span.wp-exclude-emoji` appended in one piece || 0 ||
|| the span appended inside a wrapper element || 0 ||
|| plain text appended (control) || 1 ||

Reading the source, an element or text added anywhere inside an excluded element should be replaced the same way, since its parent becomes the node passed to `parse()`; I have not tested that case.

A possible fix is to skip the node in the observer when it is inside an excluded element, for example `node.closest( '.wp-exclude-emoji' )` before `parse( node )`, or to apply `doNotParse()` to the node itself and its ancestors in `parse()`. The first keeps the change out of the vendored `twemoji.js`.

This matters for anything that inserts text the fallback should leave alone after load: editors on the front end (the reason for #52219), and code that draws emoji another way and marks it with this class. Wider context in [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/discussions/83032 Gutenberg discussion #83032].

summary: Fatal error in wp_insert_term() when the term name is not a string
XML-RPC: Fatal error when a date field is not a dateTime.iso8601
_description:
Six XML-RPC methods accept date values from the client and call `getIso()` or `getTimestamp()` on them, assuming they are IXR_Date objects. That is only true when the client sends a dateTime.iso8601 value. A client sending the date as an array for example, causes a fatal error in PHP.

This can happen with:

 * wp.editPost ( post_date, post_date_gmt, if_not_modified_since )
 * wp.newPost ( post_date, post_date_gmt )
 * wp.editComment ( date_created_gmt )
 * metaWeblog.newPost ( dateCreated, date_created_gmt )
 * metaWeblog.editPost ( dateCreated, date_created_gmt )

wp.newPost is the only one of these that accepts a string. The other four fatal on a string as well.

#28601 fixed this for strings in wp.newPost back in 4.0, but that fix only covered wp.newPost, and it still fatals there when the value is an array because it passes the value straight into date_create(). #42995 is the same fatal in wp.editComment and is still open.

It is very easy to reproduce -

{{{
curl -s http://localhost:8889/xmlrpc.php -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' --data '<?xml version="1.0"?>
<methodCall>
  <methodName>wp.editPost</methodName>
  <params>
    <param><value><int>1</int></value></param>
    <param><value><string>admin</string></value></param>
    <param><value><string>password</string></value></param>
    <param><value><int>1</int></value></param>
    <param><value><struct>
      <member><name>post_date</name><value><array><data>
        <value><string>2026-01-01 00:00:00</string></value>
      </data></array></value></member>
    </struct></value></param>
  </params>
</methodCall>'
}}}


I've got a PR that adds a single wp_xmlrpc_server::_convert_client_date() helper and uses it at each of these call sites. An IXR_Date passes through untouched, a string is converted the same way wp.newPost already does, and anything else returns a `400 IXR_Error` to the client instead of a fatal error. It also fixes #42995.

`WP_Script_Modules::add_hooks()` and `WP_Interactivity_API::add_hooks()` register their callbacks as `array( $this, 'method' )`. `wp-settings.php` calls both on `after_setup_theme` with the instance that is the global at that moment. The callbacks stay bound to that object.

summary: Add pre_wp_count_posts filter for the post counts query
_description:
`wp_count_posts()` offers no way to bypass its `GROUP BY post_status` aggregate and serve the counts from another source.

The result of `wp_count_posts()` is cached in the object cache under the key returned by `_count_posts_cache_key( $type )`. That key is deleted on **every status transition**. On a large site with frequent publishing the cache is therefore almost never warm: nearly every admin request misses and re-runs the full aggregate over the entire post type, which takes several seconds on a table with 1M+ posts.

For a large publisher, an exact real-time count in the admin dashboard is not important as long as they are able to publish without the list screen taking several seconds to load.  We can happily trade a little count accuracy for performance. 

We can run the aggregate in the background using Action Scheduler and store the result in a durable store (an option). But to make `wp_count_posts()` actually return that value and skip its query, we have to fill core's object cache by hand. On every request, we `wp_cache_set()` the stored counts under the key returned by internal `_count_posts_cache_key()` function, so core's `wp_count_posts()` hits the cache.

With a `pre_wp_count_posts` filter, `wp_count_posts()` could serve the pre-computed value (for whoever wants to trade off accuracy for performance) and skip the main query entirely.

summary: Editor: Add a background clip block support to facilitate text gradients
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77141.

Adds a `background.backgroundClip` block support, so a block can set which box its background is painted into: `border-box`, `padding-box`, `content-box`, or the `text` itself. Clipping to the text is what gives blocks a gradient text fill, since CSS has no gradient colour.

For the text value the style engine also emits `-webkit-background-clip` and
`-webkit-text-fill-color`, and the block skips the `has-background` class because
nothing paints the block's background. For the box values only the fill colour
is reset, because `-webkit-background-clip` is an alias of `background-clip` in
Chromium and resetting it would discard the value.

The setting is not part of appearance tools. A theme opts in by setting
`settings.background.backgroundClip`, either true or an array of the values it
wants to offer.

The editor controls and the `core/heading` and `core/paragraph` opt-ins arrive with
the next Gutenberg package update.

summary: Combining characters aren't normalized to Unicode Form C on output
_description:
The HTML produced by WordPress functions like `get_the_excerpt()` and `the_content()` doesn't perform any Unicode Normalization.

This lack of normalisation is problematic because the W3C recommends Normalization Form C - https://www.w3.org/TR/charmod-norm/

It is possible to wrap these functions - for example `normalizer_normalize( get_the_excerpt(), Normalizer::FORM_C );` - but this quickly becomes cumbersome in complex themes.

Would it make sense for WordPress to ensure that the content coming out of the post object is normalized before being returned?

**Test**

My blog post contains the text `Anaïs`. The `ï` is U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I and U+0308 COMBINING DIAERESIS.

When I run the output of `the_content()` through the W3C Validator, it complains

> Warning: Text run is not in Unicode Normalization Form C. 


**Background**

There's this previous ticket which talks about normalizing in the editor and on save - #30130.

However, for anyone saving plain text / markdown this doesn't seem to work. Text is saved un-normalised.

summary: Name the item, or give a count, in the plugin/theme auto-update email subject lines
_description:
Follow-up of #50268, where the current subject lines were introduced in 5.5.

The subject line of the plugin/theme auto-update email is the same regardless of how many items were updated, and never says which ones. Plugins release independently of one another, so a run that has anything to do usually has a single plugin to do it for. Among the 100 most popular plugins in the directory, the median gap between releases is around 50 days, and their most recent releases fall on 40 different days. The update check runs twice a day. So the site admin sees, over and over:

{{{
[My Site] Some plugins were automatically updated
}}}

for a body that reads:

{{{
These plugins are now up to date:
- Jetpack (from version 16.1.2 to 16.1.3) : https://wordpress.org/plugins/jetpack/
}}}

The subject carries none of the information the admin actually wants, so every one of these emails has to be opened before it can be triaged or filed. Someone running a handful of sites receives a stream of identical subjects and has no way to tell, from the inbox, which one is worth a look.

== Proposal ==

When a single item of a single type was updated, name it in the subject. Otherwise, give a count instead of the word "Some".

So the two most common emails become:

{{{
[My Site] Jetpack was automatically updated
[My Site] 3 plugins were automatically updated
}}}

Plugin and theme names are not bounded in length, and some run well past what a mail client shows. A name that long should be truncated before it goes in the subject, around 40 characters with an ellipsis.

'''Success emails''' (subject built from `$successful_updates`):

|| '''Case''' || '''Current''' || '''Proposed''' ||
|| 1 plugin || `[%s] Some plugins were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$s was automatically updated` ||
|| N plugins || `[%s] Some plugins were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins were automatically updated` ||
|| 1 theme || `[%s] Some themes were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$s was automatically updated` ||
|| N themes || `[%s] Some themes were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d themes were automatically updated` ||
|| plugins + themes || `[%s] Some plugins and themes have automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins and %3$d themes were automatically updated` ||

'''Failure and mixed emails''' (subject built from `$failed_updates`, as it is today):

|| '''Case''' || '''Current''' || '''Proposed''' ||
|| 1 plugin || `[%s] Some plugins have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$s failed to update` ||
|| N plugins || `[%s] Some plugins have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins have failed to update` ||
|| 1 theme || `[%s] Some themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$s failed to update` ||
|| N themes || `[%s] Some themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d themes have failed to update` ||
|| plugins + themes || `[%s] Some plugins and themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins and %3$d themes have failed to update` ||

The email body is unchanged in every case.

Sites can already do all of this through the `auto_plugin_theme_update_email` filter, but the default is what the great majority of admins actually receive, and the information is right there when the subject is built.

Related: #50268, #50350, #51695, #53049

|| 2.7 || 70 || 0.039 || `WP_Test_REST_Tags_Controller` ||
|| 2.6 || 49 || 0.054 || `Tests_REST_WpRestTemplatesController` ||

Two profiles appear, and they need different fixes. `Tests_WpTokenMap` and `Tests_Canonical_PostStatus` are data-provider matrices of cheap tests, so the lever is the size of the matrix. `Tests_Admin_ExportWp` and `Tests_Image_Editor_Imagick` are a few expensive tests, so the lever is fixture and I/O cost inside each one.

== How to work a class ==

 1. Claim it in a comment here, one class at a time.
 2. Measure before: `npm run test:php -- --filter Class_Name`, then read the `time` attributes in `tests/phpunit/build/logs/junit.xml`.
 3. Apply the levers the handbook already documents: hoist immutable fixtures into `wpSetUpBeforeClass()`, share expensive objects across the class, trim provider matrices that exercise identical code paths, and mock file or image work where the assertion does not need the real thing.
 4. Measure after, the same way, and post both numbers on this ticket with the PR.

Guardrails: no assertion is removed to save time, no expected value changes to make a test pass, no timeouts are raised, and a test that protects a specific behavior stays even if it is slow.

Related: #42904, #42278 and #41451 (older performance proposals that can now be evaluated against data), #63026 (the bcrypt precedent), #52645, #65887.

summary: Tests: Let WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase reflect read-only routes
_description:
Follow-up to #40538, splitting out the structural half so it can land on its own.

== The problem ==

`WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase` declares nine abstract methods (`tests/phpunit/includes/testcase-rest-controller.php`, lines 24–40 on trunk today):

{{{
test_register_routes()   test_context_param()    test_get_items()
test_get_item()          test_create_item()      test_update_item()
test_delete_item()       test_prepare_item()     test_get_item_schema()
}}}

Every controller test must implement all nine. A read-only controller has no create, update or delete route, so those three methods have nothing to assert. Since [53921] and [54058] the accepted way out has been `@doesNotPerformAssertions`, with the note that it "can be reconsidered in the future".

That has not stayed flat. Trunk today carries 101 `@doesNotPerformAssertions` annotations in 26 files, and 98 of them are REST controller tests. Twenty files sit under `tests/phpunit/tests/rest-api/`, plus three under `fonts/font-library/`, two under `icons/`, and one unrelated case in `user/passwordHash.php`. Each new read-only controller inherits the pattern on the day it is written.

== Options ==

 1. '''Default implementations that assert the negative.''' Make the six operation methods non-abstract, with a default that dispatches the operation against the controller's collection and item routes and asserts it is rejected (`rest_no_route`, or the controller's documented error). A controller that supports the operation overrides the method as today. This turns 98 no-ops into real assertions with one change and no per-file work, and it stops the count growing.
 2. '''A read-only base class.''' A second testcase with the read-side methods only, and controllers pick the one that fits. Cleaner signature, but every existing read-only controller test has to move, and nothing stops a future controller extending the wrong one.
 3. '''Leave the abstract alone''' and keep annotating. The status quo.

Option 1 seems the best trade, but the default needs care: some controllers register a route and reject the method with 403 or 405 rather than `rest_no_route`, and the schema for a POST body differs per controller. A first patch could dispatch and accept any error response, then tighten.

Once the base class change lands, the remaining annotations outside the abstract methods are a per-case read, which stays on #40538.

Related: #40538, #41463, #55652, [53921], [54058].

summary: Database tests fail on MariaDB 13.1 because utf8 now resolves to utf8mb4
_description:
Reported by @danielblack in [https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02RQBWTW/p1788847795453089 core Slack].

MariaDB 13.1.1 removes UTF8_IS_UTF8MB3 from the default old_mode ([https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-30041 MDEV-30041]), so the charset name utf8 now means utf8mb4 instead of utf8mb3 in DDL and SET NAMES. This breaks 4 tests in Tests_DB_Charset (seen on MariaDB's own [https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/505/builds/8348/steps/4/logs/stdio WordPress buildbot]): test_get_table_charset, test_get_column_charset, test_strip_invalid_text_from_query, and test_set_charset_changes_the_connection_collation. 

They fail because the test file's $utf8_is_utf8mb3 flag (tests/phpunit/tests/db/charset.php:62-66) is set by a version check ("MariaDB ≥ 10.6.1"), which only accounts for the 10.6 change in how the server reports the charset, not the 13.1 change in what the name utf8 creates. Core's runtime is fine — wpdb::determine_charset() has upgraded utf8 to utf8mb4 since 4.6 — this is purely a test-expectation fix.

get_plugins() cache ignores extra_plugin_headers registered after the first scan
_description:
`get_plugins()` stores plugin headers in the `plugins` object cache on the first scan. `get_file_data()` applies `extra_plugin_headers` only while that scan reads files. A later `get_plugins()` hits the cache and never sees headers registered in between.

That first scan often happens during plugin include, before `plugins_loaded`. Any plugin that calls `get_plugins()` there freezes a snapshot with no extra headers. Plugins that register extra headers and then read them get empty values, notices on missing keys, or skip their own update logic.

=== Reproduction ===

1. Plugin A, slug sorting before plugin B, calls `get_plugins()` in the main file (include time).
2. Plugin B adds a header on `extra_plugin_headers` and later calls `get_plugins()`.
3. Plugin B's extra header key is missing from the cached rows.

`get_plugins( '/some-slug' )` is a separate cache slot today, so a folder scan does not reuse a warm all-plugins list and can freeze the same stale headers on its own key.

=== Expected ===

Extra headers registered after the first scan should appear on the next `get_plugins()` call. Already-cached fields (Name, Version, ...) should stay. A folder argument should scan only that folder. `SHORTINIT` should not prime this cache; only `get_plugins()` should fill it.

=== Seen in the wild ===

[https://github.com/sybrew/troy/issues/24 Troy Client #24]. Troy Client registers custom plugin headers and uses them to talk to Troy Server and to keep Troy plugins off wordpress.org's update-check. An early `get_plugins()` meant those headers never landed, so Client could not see its own plugins. Client 1.8.1184 flushes the cache as a workaround. Core should not require that.

WooCommerce has hit the same cache for years. The Helper needs a `Woo:` extra header to see paid extensions (subscriptions and Woo.com updates). `WC tested up to` / `WC requires at least` also vanish, so extensions look untested. Woo already flushes `wp_cache` group `plugins` when those keys are missing (WooCommerce PRs: [https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/pull/26358 #26358], [https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/pull/21669 #21669]). That is a product workaround for this core bug. They knew about the bug, so I'm surprised that they didn't raise an issue with WordPress.

Plugin authors should not have to detect missing keys and flush the `plugins` cache themselves. A core fix does that work once. Sites that update WordPress then see extra headers on the next `get_plugins()` call, so custom update-server connections this cache bug severed start working again without a plugin update.

Themes cannot cause this. They load after `plugins_loaded`.

summary: Editor: Migrate the Column block to the width block support
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/76684.

Migrates the Column block from its ad-hoc width attribute to the standard
dimensions.width block support, so column widths can be set from global styles
and theme.json while existing columns keep working.

Columns sit in a flex container and size themselves with flex-basis rather than
width, so WP_Theme_JSON converts the computed width declaration and sets
flex-grow to 0. This covers the block level, block style variations, and
variation styles set within a responsive breakpoint.

The block.json and theme.json changes arrive with the next Gutenberg package
update, as they did for the Button block in #65388.

summary: Unauthenticated XML-RPC pingback timing oracle discloses non-public post titles and privacy-request email addresses
_description:
**This issue is being posted to Trac for public discussion at the WordPress Security Team's explicit request.**

The security team said to post this to Trac and to mention that "the Security Team recommended public discussion".

An unauthenticated user can perform a pingback for a non-public pingback-enabled post using regex matching on the post title. If there is a post which has a title that matches the regex, then WordPress sleeps for one second and performs an outbound HTTP request, even if the matching post is one that the unauthenticated user cannot read (e.g. draft, scheduled, and trashed posts). The timing differential and outbound HTTP request can be observed, allowing the user to do character-by-character enumeration of pingback-enabled post titles that the user should not have access to. Disclosure of the title of an unavailable post may have a confidentiality impact.

After submitting the report to the security team, we found that this pingback-enabled primitive was publicly discussed in [https://www.imperva.com/blog/beware-a-threat-actor-could-steal-the-titles-of-your-private-and-draft-wordpress-posts/ Beware! A threat actor could steal the titles of your private (and draft) WordPress posts with this new vulnerability!] by Imperva (2025).

An unauthenticated user can attempt to perform a pingback for a non-public non-pingback-enabled post using regex matching on the post title. If there is a post which has a title that matches the regex, WordPress does not explicitly sleep or perform an outbound HTTP request as it does in the case where the post is pingback-enabled. However, there is a divergence in code that is executed in the case where the regex matches a post title v.s the case where the regex does not match a post title. This codepath divergence creates a timing differential. The unauthenticated user can use multicall to perform many pingback attempts within one request, amplifying the timing differential.

This second primitive can be used to do time-based character-by-character enumeration of non-pingback-enabled post titles that the user should not have access to. Importantly, this includes user email addresses for which a data export or data erasure has been performed, as these processes create non-public non-pingback-enabled posts with the user's email address in the post title. This represents a confidentiality and privacy impact.

The original report is attached. The issue was discovered by GPT 5.6 Sol, and the report was written by GPT 5.6 Sol with human editing and validation. We have chosen to withhold publication of the proof of concept scripts for the time being.

**This issue is being posted to Trac for public discussion at the WordPress Security Team's explicit request.**

summary: Build PHPStan extensions for query-string $args passed to wp_parse_args()-based template tags
_description:
Follow-up to #65817, where r63440 and r63441 gave the dual-mode template tags conditional `@phpstan-return` annotations so that consuming the result of a call that only prints is reported as an error. As mentioned in a [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13371/changes#r3937932277 PR comment], those annotations cannot describe one case: an `$args` passed as a query string. This ticket proposes two PHPStan extensions to close that gap, and reports a survey of how often the query-string form is actually used in core, in themes and in plugins. == The problem == Around two dozen template tags accept `$args` as either an array or a URL-encoded query string, which `wp_parse_args()` runs through `wp_parse_str()` (which also come to find out has a `wp_parse_str` filter). A conditional return type keys off the '''static type of the argument at the call site''', so an array shape can be matched but a string cannot: {{{#!php true ) ); // Undecidable: 'echo=0' is a ConstantStringType, never a subtype of any array shape. $html = wp_list_authors( 'echo=0' ); }}} Every such tag therefore ends its conditional with a branch that leaves the type a union so nothing is reported either way. For most tags that branch reads `string|null`. For `wp_dropdown_languages()` it has to read `string|void`, because that function bails with a bare `return;` rather than `return null;` — putting `void` back inside a union, which is the thing [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13359 previous] [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13371 PRs] set out to eliminate. PHPStan offers no hook to customize how `X is Y` is decided inside a conditional type, so this cannot be fixed in a docblock. It needs an extension. == Survey: core == All 61 functions in `src/` documented `array|string` (or `string|array`) that call `wp_parse_args()` were identified, then narrowed to the 24 free functions where argument 1 is the args. Every call site in `src/` and `tests/phpunit/` was then classified. ||= First argument =||= Call sites =|| || Array literal || 61 || || Variable or expression || 420 || || No argument || 196 || || '''String literal''' || '''18''' || The 18 string call sites: ||= Area =||= Count =||= Detail =|| || Bundled legacy themes || 14 || 13 of them `the_title_attribute( 'echo=0' )` in Twenty Ten through Twenty Sixteen, plus `wp_get_archives( 'type=monthly' )` in Twenty Ten || || Tests || 3 || `get_pages()`, `get_posts()`, `wp_list_pages()` || || `src/wp-includes/theme-compat/sidebar.php` || 1 || `wp_list_pages( 'title_li=

' . __( 'Pages' ) . '

' )` || '''`src/wp-includes` proper and `src/wp-admin` contain no query-string call sites at all.''' The single non-theme instance is in `theme-compat/`, itself legacy scaffolding. The practical consequence is that the undecidable branch costs core's own analysis almost nothing. Its entire effect lands on themes and plugins, which consume these annotations through [https://github.com/php-stubs/wordpress-stubs php-stubs/wordpress-stubs]. == Survey: themes == Measured across the 14,941 themes in the WordPress.org directory. ||= Function =||= Array form =||= Query-string form =||= Themes with at least one =|| || `the_title_attribute` || 1,876 || '''4,329''' || 1,280 || || `wp_list_categories` || 2,114 || '''1,815''' || 1,444 || || `wp_get_archives` || 2,919 || '''1,696''' || 1,000 || || `wp_list_pages` || 986 || '''1,482''' || 1,032 || || `wp_list_comments` || 6,779 || 726 || 583 || || `wp_tag_cloud` || 243 || '''484''' || 445 || || `wp_link_pages` || 21,327 || 439 || 184 || || `wp_list_bookmarks` || 18 || '''292''' || 272 || || `wp_dropdown_categories` || 453 || 223 || 215 || || `wp_page_menu` || 375 || 60 || 53 || || `paginate_comments_links` || 158 || 57 || 47 || || `wp_list_authors` || 5 || 30 || 24 || The idiom is not confined to abandoned themes. It ships today in GeneratePress (500k installs), Lightning (100k), Hestia (80k), Twenty Ten (50k), Ashe (30k), Hueman (20k) and Rife Free (20k), as well as in core's own bundled themes. == Survey: plugins == Measured across the 74,641 plugins in the WordPress.org directory. Roughly 650 query-string call sites across 350 to 400 distinct plugins. ||= Function =||= Array form =||= Query-string form =|| || `the_title_attribute` || 276 || '''289''' || || `wp_dropdown_categories` || 850 || 95 || || `wp_list_pages` || 60 || '''90''' || || `wp_get_archives` || 23 || '''50''' || || `wp_list_categories` || 82 || 41 || || `wp_dropdown_pages` || 647 || 28 || || `wp_list_comments` || 146 || 14 || || `wp_tag_cloud` || 32 || 11 || || `wp_dropdown_users` || 280 || 10 || || `wp_link_pages` || 183 || 8 || || `wp_list_authors` || 16 || 8 || || `wp_list_bookmarks` || 4 || 4 || || `wp_page_menu` || 2 || 0 || That is around 0.5% of the whole directory, but roughly 10 to 20% of the plugins that call these functions at all. Actively maintained, high-install plugins still use it: GenerateBlocks (200k), YARPP (100k), VK All in One Expansion Unit (100k), WPtouch (60k), Easy Digital Downloads (40k). == Method and caveats == * Core figures come from a scan of `src/` and `tests/phpunit/`, excluding bundled third-party libraries. The scan is multi-line aware; a second line-based pass produced identical totals. * Theme and plugin figures were gathered by regex search over indexed copies of both directories, matching the function name followed by `(` and then either a quote (query-string form) or `array(`/`[` (array form). * '''Those searches are line-scoped''', so a call whose `array(` sits on the following line is counted in neither column. The leakage was measured for two functions: 247 additional multi-line array calls for `wp_dropdown_categories()` and 405 for `wp_dropdown_pages()`. The '''percentages''' above therefore overstate the query-string share; the '''absolute counts''' are sound. * Args passed through a variable are counted in neither column, so query-string figures are a floor rather than a ceiling. * Only the latest indexed version of each theme and plugin was searched. * Query-string matches were manually sampled to discard commented-out code, docblock examples, hook and callback names, and calls whose first parameter is not the args. == Proposal: two extensions == These are two distinct PHPStan extension points, best implemented together because they share one table of metadata: for each supported function, which parameter carries the args and what its `$defaults` array contains. === 1. A dynamic return type extension === A `PHPStan\Type\DynamicFunctionReturnTypeExtension`, the same interface already used in this repo by `tests/phpstan/ApplyFiltersDynamicFunctionReturnTypeExtension.php`. For a supported call it inspects the argument type via `Scope::getType()` and: * `ConstantStringType` — runs `parse_str()` on the literal during analysis, merges the result over the function's defaults, evaluates the same branch logic the docblock encodes, and returns `VoidType`, `StringType` or whatever that branch resolves to. * `ConstantArrayType` — the same merge and the same decision, replacing what the conditional does today. * anything else — returns null so the docblock type stands. This makes `the_title_attribute( 'echo=0' )` resolve to exactly `string` and `wp_dropdown_languages( 'id=0' )` resolve to exactly `void`, removing the undecidable branch for literal arguments. === 2. A rule forbidding non-array `$args` === A `PHPStan\Rules\Rule` that reports passing anything other than an array to these parameters. Unlike the inference extension it does not need the value to be knowable, so it also covers concatenated and interpolated strings. 👉 Functions which are passed a query string could trigger a `_doing_it_wrong()` to encourage passing args arrays as they can more readily be statically-analyzed. === Why both === Only a bare literal is a `ConstantStringType`. Anything built up loses its value: ||= Expression =||= Type PHPStan sees =||= Extension can resolve? =|| || `'echo=0'` || `'echo=0'` || yes || || `'title_li=' . $x` || `non-falsy-string` || no || || `"type=$foo"` || `non-falsy-string` || no || The dominant list-tag idiom is concatenation (`'title_li=&echo=0&child_of=' . $id`), so inference alone leaves much of the ecosystem untyped. The rule covers those. Conversely the rule cannot improve a type, so it does nothing for the annotations. They are complementary. Both of core's own non-theme string call sites are concatenations or interpolations, so the inference extension would do nothing for either; only the rule reaches them. == Side finding: a live bug the rule would catch == 28 themes still call `wp_link_pages()` with its pre-2.1 positional signature: {{{#!php Pages: ', '

', 'number' ); }}} `wp_link_pages()` has no positional back-compat handling. The second and third arguments are discarded, and `parse_str( '

Pages: ' )` yields the single junk key `'

Pages:_' => ''`, so every default survives and the theme silently renders default markup instead of its own. Inference can never flag this, since the string is not a valid args string in the first place. A rule forbidding non-array args reports it immediately. == Open questions == 1. '''Where should these live?''' In `tests/phpstan/` they only help core analyze itself, where the survey shows there is almost nothing to find. To reach the themes and plugins that actually use the idiom they would need to ship in [https://github.com/szepeviktor/phpstan-wordpress szepeviktor/phpstan-wordpress] or alongside php-stubs/wordpress-stubs. That argues for developing them outside core, with core consuming them. 2. '''Soundness.''' `wp_parse_str()` applies a `wp_parse_str` filter to the parsed result, and a few tags filter `$args` before parsing — `wp_get_archives()` runs `apply_filters( 'wp_get_archives_args', $args )` ahead of `wp_parse_args()`, and `get_calendar()` filters afterwards. Only two plugins in the directory filter `wp_parse_str` at all, so that hook is not a practical concern, but `wp_get_archives()` and `get_calendar()` may warrant exclusion from the inference extension. 3. '''Defaults drift.''' The metadata table duplicates each function's `$defaults`. A test asserting the table matches the source would prevent it going stale, unless the defaults can be extracted from the call to `wp_parse_args()` at runtime. 4. '''Should the rule be adopted by core at all?''' It would flag one file in `theme-compat/`, three test call sites and the bundled legacy themes. That is cheap, but it mostly enforces a state core has already reached. == Not proposed here == A `wp_parse_args()` return type extension, typing `$parsed_args` inside these functions as a precise shape rather than `array`, would remove a good deal of `mixed`-related noise in their bodies. That is a separate concern and does not affect call-site resolution, since the conditional keys off the caller's argument. ---- 🤖 ''This ticket was drafted with help of Claude Opus 5.''

summary: Multiple runs of the Test Old Branches workflow in a short period of time can cause a stampede of automatic reruns and Slack notifications
_description:
GitHub Actions workflows are configured to automatically rerun when the first run attempt is cancelled or fails. They are also configured so that when the triggering event for a run is not `pull_request` the `concurrency.group` value is `WORKFLOWNAME-SHA`. Because old branches do not receive updates often, the runs triggered by `workflow_dispatch` usually have the same concurrency value for m any consecutive runs.

When the Test Old Branches workflow runs more than once in short period of time, this causes a cascade of cancellations, re-runs, and Slack notifications. Consider the following example:

- Commit made to `trunk` that runs Test Old Branches workflow.
- Run 1 starts
- Second commit made to `trunk` that runs Test Old Branches workflow.
- Run 2 starts
- Incomplete runs triggered by the first commit are cancelled based on the concurrency group
- Run 1 is restarted
- Incomplete runs triggered by the second commit are cancelled based on the concurrency group
- Run 2 is restarted
- Incomplete runs triggered by the first commit are cancelled for the second time based on the concurrency group
- Run 1 cancellations send a Slack notification to raise awareness.

This is then made worse because a successful run following a cancelled or failed run is considered "fixed", which is also a scenario where a Slack notification is pushed.

With 25+ branches eligible to receive security updates as a courtesy, this means that roughly 150 workflow runs are triggered every time the Test Old Branches workflow runs (using 25 branches * 6 workflows each, which is a rough average) and potentially roughly the same number of notifications for cancellations, then the same number for "fixes". This can be even worse if the commit made in `trunk` caused legitimate failures or also experienced timeouts/cancellations, and when a number of other commits are made around the same time.

The cancelled run Slack notification is configured to only send a notice for only the second run attempt to avoid needlessly sharing a timeout that resolves itself during the automatic re-run (see r62740). However, the `cancelled` outcome in GitHub Actions represents a few different outcomes that are not easy to clarify. A cancellation could be a timeout, a user initiated cancellation, a concurrency-based cancellation, and sometimes a platform-level problem can cause cancellations.

Because of this there's no logic included to determine if the cancellation was caused by the configured concurrency groupings, which is an expected and desired outcome and does not warrant a rerun or Slack notification.

[https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02RQBWTW/p1788446249310839 See this Slack history] for an example of how this materializes in #core.

summary: Classic Editor: `postboxes.add_postbox_toggles()`'s jQuery UI `.sortable()` init hangs the main thread indefinitely in Safari 26.0.1 (WebKit 605.1.15)
_description:
On a stock WordPress 7.1 install — default theme (Twenty Twenty-Five), zero plugins — opening any
post or page in the Classic Editor in Safari 26.0.1 on macOS hangs the browser tab's main thread
completely between `DOMContentLoaded` and `window.load`. The tab becomes fully unresponsive: no
scroll, no focus, no typing, no further script execution. Chrome and Firefox on the same machine
load the same screen normally. The block editor is unaffected in Safari.

This reproduces on the single default "Hello world!" post with no custom fields, no extra meta
boxes, and no plugins active, so it is not specific to any plugin, theme, or content type — it's in
WordPress core's own admin JS interacting with Safari 26.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Fresh (or default-content) WordPress 7.1 install, default theme, no plugins active.
2. In Safari 26.0.1 on macOS, log in to wp-admin and open `post.php?post=1&action=edit` (or any
   post/page) — forced into the Classic Editor if the block editor is the default (e.g. via the
   Classic Editor plugin, or `add_filter('use_block_editor_for_post', '__return_false')`).
3. Watch the page: it paints, then the tab locks up before `load` fires. No user input registers.

**Isolation / root cause**

Bisected with an instrumented mu-plugin (PHP + browser lifecycle logging: heartbeat, rAF-gap and
main-thread-stall detection, per-request script/style dequeue and stub knobs) driving real Safari
via `safaridriver` for a deterministic HANG/OK verdict per trial (~20s/trial, ~40+ trials run).

- The hang sits in `wp-admin/js/post.js`'s `jQuery(document).ready` handler, specifically the
  statement immediately after `new ClipboardJS('.copy-attachment-url.edit-media')`
  (`wp-admin/js/post.js`, around line 315): `postboxes.add_postbox_toggles(pagenow);` (line 319).
- Inside `wp-admin/js/postbox.js`, `add_postbox_toggles()` calls `init()`, which runs
  `jQuery('.meta-box-sortables').sortable({ ..., forcePlaceholderSize: true, ... })` (jQuery UI
  Sortable).
- Decisive test: with the rest of `add_postbox_toggles()` left completely intact (its click-handler
  bindings for `.hndle`, `.handlediv`, `.hide-postbox-tog`, etc. all still run normally) and *only*
  `jQuery.fn.sortable` replaced with a no-op (`function(){ return this; }`) immediately before it
  would otherwise run, the hang disappears entirely — the page reaches `readyState: complete` and
  fires `load` normally. Every trial that leaves the real `.sortable()` call in place hangs;
  every trial that skips only that call does not. This isolates the loop to jQuery UI Sortable's
  own initialization (likely its internal geometry read/write for `forcePlaceholderSize` and
  per-item height calculation across `.meta-box-sortables`/`.postbox`), not to WordPress's own code
  around it.
- Removing all page CSS also prevents the hang, which rules out a pure logic loop (e.g. a bad
  `while` condition) and points at a layout-dependent loop: something in Sortable's init reads a
  geometry property (`outerHeight()`/`offsetHeight`), the browser performs a synchronous layout
  pass, and — specifically under Safari 26's WebKit engine — the loop never resolves. Google Chrome
  (Blink) does not reproduce it at all. An older Playwright WebKit build (2336) also does not
  reproduce it, suggesting this is a very recent WebKit/Safari 26 regression rather than a
  long-standing Sortable bug — though I have not identified a specific WebKit engine change or
  Bugzilla ticket to point to; I could not find one on a search of WebKit Bugzilla and would
  welcome a WebKit engineer's read on this from the WordPress side.
- This is unrelated to Advanced Custom Fields or any other plugin: initially observed on 4
  ACF-driven pages and suspected to involve ACF's `acf_after_title` field-group position, but that
  hypothesis was tested and disproved (forcing the field group to a standard `normal` position did
  not fix it), and the hang was then reproduced on a completely stock post with all plugins
  deactivated and the default Twenty Twenty-Five theme active.

**Environment**

- WordPress 7.1

summary: REST API: let the media create endpoint record the attachment an upload was edited from
_description:
''Claude Code drafted this ticket from the Gutenberg change, forwarded along:''

> With client-side media processing, Gutenberg is moving image edits (crop, rotate, flip) from the server `media/<id>/edit` endpoint into the browser: the edit is applied with libvips and the result is uploaded through `POST /wp/v2/media` as a new attachment, the same way the editor has always created edited images. See https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/82362 (fixes https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/82295, where server-side edits strip the gain map from HDR JPEGs).
>
> One thing the `/edit` endpoint does that the upload endpoint cannot is record where the new image came from: it stores a `parent_image` entry (`attachment_id` and the source's relative `file` path) in the new attachment's metadata, copies the source's EXIF `image_meta` for any field the new file lacks, and resets the orientation to 1. Edits made in the browser should relate to their source the same way.
>
> Proposed change: add an optional `parent_image` integer parameter to the media create endpoint. When set, it must reference an existing image attachment the current user can edit (matching the `/edit` permission check), and after the upload the new attachment's metadata gets the same `parent_image` entry and EXIF carry-over that `edit_media_item()` writes. Without the parameter nothing changes.
>
> Related: #65367 (client-side media processing endpoints).

Patch incoming.

What's proposed in this ticket is a smaller, incremental step that enables user customization and builds upon existing support for color schemes and design system theming.

**Design Notes:**

The attached image can give an idea of how it could be integrated into the existing settings. It is not a design proposal (I am not a designer) and I'd welcome design input on a final design.

This should also integrate with site editor improvements in r62454 ([https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/78397 Gutenberg#78397]).

Generated styles for wp-admin interface elements may use parts of [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/tree/trunk/packages/theme `@wordpress/theme`], either the ThemeProvider itself (React-based) or [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/tree/trunk/packages/theme/src/color-ramps internal color ramp logic], which may require changes in the package to expose this as a generalized JavaScript utility not bound to React.

Remove the admin menu auto-fold feature & move responsive viewport trigger to 960px.
_description:
Since slightly before the dawn of time (definitely before r20749, but hard to pin down exactly when), the admin menu has automatically collapsed to a reduced width icon-only display on small viewports.

Originally, this occurred on viewports smaller than 900px; later that was expanded to be below 960px. 

When the responsive state of the admin menu was introduced in WordPress 3.8 as part of the MP6 redesign, the scope of the auto-fold behavior was limited to between 782px and 960px.

On today's devices, those widths only occur in a handful of limited scenarios: intentionally narrowed viewports, iPad Air in portrait mode, and smaller iPad Pro devices in portrait mode are the primary cases.

The collapsed menu can still be useful for some users, and this is not proposing to remove the ability to fold the menu; but the automatic folding behavior is now obsolete.

This proposal is limited to removing the behavior that automatically triggers a folded menu & to move the trigger for the responsive menu to happen at 960px.

This would help resolve issues like #46307, in that this menu would only ever appear if a user has explicitly made the choice to use it, and they would be able to change that choice if they needed clarification on a specific item in the menu. Right now, if you are inside that narrow viewport range, your only option for the menu is a version that has no visible labels at the top level and can be difficult to understand.

summary: Race condition in WordPress 7.1 Block Editor: Adding custom field to auto-draft causes duplicated postmeta and forces comment_status to closed
_description:
In WordPress 7.1, a race condition occurs when adding a custom field (via the legacy Custom Fields meta box) to a newly created post (auto-draft status) before its initial save or publish. This results in two critical issues:

* The custom field is inserted twice in the `wp_postmeta` table.
* The `comment_status` is incorrectly forced to `closed`, regardless of the site's default settings.

== Steps to Reproduce ==

1. Go to '''Posts > Add New Post''' to open the Block Editor (creating an auto-draft).
2. Ensure the legacy "Custom Fields" panel is enabled.
3. Before saving as a draft or publishing, immediately add a new custom field and value.
4. Click '''Publish''' or '''Save Draft'''.
5. Check the post metadata and discussion settings.

== Expected Behavior ==

* The custom field should be saved only once.
* The post's `comment_status` should inherit the site's default setting (usually `open`).

== Actual Behavior ==

* The custom field is duplicated (two identical key-value pairs in `wp_postmeta`).
* The `comment_status` changes to `closed`.
